title: Deep in one: Revelation
subtitle: Twelve sessions in the Bible's last book: how apocalyptic writing works, the four ways of reading it, and the slain Lamb on the throne, heard first as its churches heard it.
intro: Revelation has been read in more ways than almost any book of the Bible. It has steadied martyrs, filled hymnbooks and cathedral windows, and been used to name dates that came and went. This track reads it in order, a chapter or a few chapters at a time, and asks first what John's visions meant to seven real churches in the Roman province of Asia, under pressure and tempted to make their peace with Rome. Only then does it ask what they mean for you.

Each session opens a chapter in the Study Bible with its notes in plain words, and most also open a film, a doctrine or a guide. Where faithful Christians read the book differently, the track sets the readings side by side and leaves the question open. The book's own purpose is plain enough: it was written so that its readers would worship the Lamb and endure. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Revelation. The group meets twelve times and reads a chapter or a few chapters each time, from the vision of Christ to the new heaven and the new earth. It suits people who have avoided the book, people who were frightened by it as children, and people who have read it with a chart beside them. The leader's task is to keep the group in the text and in the first readers' world, and to let the book do what it was written to do: lead people to worship the Lamb and to endure.

Each person reads the chapters, their notes and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads the key passage aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for twelve meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A leader doesn't need to have settled every question about Revelation. A leader needs to have read the chapters and their notes, to be fair to readings other than their own, and to be willing to say they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit round a table if you can, with the chapters open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Revelation was written to be read aloud to gathered churches, so read it aloud, and let a different voice take each scene. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that the group will not argue anyone into a view of the end times.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: read the key passage aloud, sharing the reading, and let a minute of quiet follow it.
Thirty minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask first what the passage meant to the churches of Asia.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words, or a song from the chapter read aloud together.
Five minutes: name the next chapters and the page the session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Revelation raises hard questions at almost every turn: what the numbers mean, who the beasts are, whether the judgments are just, when Christ will return and what the thousand years are. When the group reaches one, read the note on it together before anyone answers. Set out the main readings, preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist, and the millennial views, each in the form its own defenders would sign, and don't press the group to choose. Faithful Christians who confess the same creed have disagreed here for centuries.

Some people will want to match the visions to this week's news or to set a date. Treat the wish kindly, and point back to the first readers and to the words of Jesus that no one knows the day or the hour. Some will come with fear left over from preaching they heard as children. Listen to that, and let the book's own purpose answer it: Revelation was written to steady the faithful, not to terrify them.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Revelation was written to people under pressure, and some in the group will be under pressure too: grieving, ill, mistreated at work or at home, or carrying a fear of judgment that will not lift. When someone speaks of that, stop the discussion and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry to the new creation. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

Never use the book's judgments to threaten anyone, or to suggest that someone's suffering is a punishment. If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief or low mood that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, a fear of God or of the end that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: How to read Revelation
teaching: Revelation's first word in Greek is apokalypsis, an unveiling. The book isn't a code to be cracked so much as a curtain drawn back, so that suffering churches could see their world as heaven sees it. John writes in a kind of literature his first readers knew well, full of symbols, numbers and beasts, the same family as the second half of Daniel. In that kind of writing seven speaks of completeness and a beast stands for an empire. The book is also a prophecy and a letter, sent to churches with names and addresses, and it promises a blessing to whoever reads it aloud and keeps it. That promise assumes ordinary believers could understand it.

Christians have read the book in four main ways. Preterists read most of it as fulfilled in the first centuries, in the judgment on Jerusalem and on Rome. Historicists read it as a map of church history from John's day to the end. Futurists read most of chapters 4 to 22 as still to come, in the years before Christ returns. Idealists read it as a picture of the struggle in every age between the Lamb and the powers that oppose him. Each reading has serious defenders and sees something true, and many readers combine them. This track leaves that question open and asks a smaller one each week: what did this mean to the churches who first heard it read aloud?

open.label: Reading Revelation and Daniel
open.why: What an apocalypse is, how its visions, symbols and numbers work, and the four main schools of reading Revelation with the history of each.

also.label: Revelation in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote Revelation and when, the setting on Patmos and in the cities of Roman Asia, and the shape of the whole book.

also.label: Revelation: the Lamb on the throne
also.why: The whole book in a few pictures: the letters to seven churches, the throne, the Lamb who was slain, the ways Christians read it, and all things made new.

also.label: The Bible's timeline
also.why: The Bible's timeline, where Revelation's own entries show how the early church weighed who wrote the book and whether it belonged among the accepted books.

sessions.question: When you have heard Revelation talked about before, was it with dread, with fascination, or hardly at all, and what did that leave you thinking about the book?
sessions.do: Read Revelation 1 to 3 aloud in one sitting this week, the way the first churches heard it. Write down the pictures that stay with you, and one thing you expected the book to say that it doesn't.

verse.text: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near.

group.open: What is the first thing that comes to mind when someone mentions the book of Revelation?
discuss: The book promises a blessing to those who read it aloud and keep it. What does that suggest about who it was written for?
Of the four ways of reading the book, which have you met before, and what does each one help you see?
Why might it matter to ask what a vision meant to its first hearers before asking what it means now?
group.pray: Give thanks that God speaks to ordinary believers, and ask that the group would read this book with humility, patience and a readiness to worship.

sessions.title: Revelation 1 and the vision of Christ
teaching: John was on Patmos, a small island off the coast of what is now Turkey, “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (Revelation 1:9). Most readers take that to mean exile. He calls himself his readers' brother and partner in tribulation, kingdom and perseverance, three words the book holds together. Before a single beast appears, it shows Jesus: “the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1:5). Those titles steadied churches whose witness could cost them their lives, and they quietly corrected an empire that thought the kings of the earth answered to Rome.

Then John turns to see the voice and finds the risen Christ standing among seven lampstands, which the chapter itself explains are the seven churches. The picture borrows from Daniel's vision of one like a son of man, and from Daniel's Ancient of Days, so that Jesus has the white hair Daniel gave to God himself. John falls at his feet as though dead. The first thing Christ does in the book is lay his right hand on a frightened man and tell him not to be afraid. Whatever follows in Revelation, that hand comes first.

open.label: Revelation 1, passage by passage
open.why: John on Patmos, the greeting to the seven churches and the vision of the risen Christ among the lampstands, explained in plain words.

also.label: Follow a verse
also.why: Follow the verses of Revelation 1 back to Daniel and the prophets, where most of the book's pictures first appear.

also.label: Christ exalted
also.why: What the Bible teaches about Christ raised, ascended and reigning, the Jesus John sees standing among the churches.

also.label: Who Jesus is
also.why: Who Jesus is in seven pictures, a way to set the risen Christ of chapter 1 beside the Jesus of the Gospels.

sessions.question: The first thing Christ does in the book is touch a frightened man and speak to him. What would change if that were what you expected of him?
sessions.do: Read Revelation 1:9 to 20 slowly. List every detail of the risen Christ, and next to each one write a word for what it tells you about him.

verse.text: When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man. But He placed His right hand on me and said, “Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.”

group.open: When have you been given a word of comfort at a moment you were sure you would be told off?
discuss: John calls himself a partner in tribulation, kingdom and perseverance. Why might those three belong together?
Jesus is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. Which of those titles do you most need, and why?
The lampstands are the churches, and Christ walks among them. What does that say about how he sees an ordinary congregation?
group.pray: Thank Christ for his nearness to his churches, and ask that each person would hear his word not to be afraid in the place where they are most afraid now.

care: Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 2 and four of the churches
teaching: The seven cities lay roughly in a loop along a road inland from the coast, so a messenger could carry the book from one to the next. Each letter opens with a picture of Christ from chapter 1, says what he knows, praises what it can, names what is wrong, and ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, and every church hears all seven. Ephesus has worked hard and tested false teachers and has abandoned its first love. Smyrna is poor and slandered, and Christ calls it rich. Pergamum lives where Satan's throne sits and has held fast, yet tolerates teaching that makes peace with idolatry. Thyatira is growing in love and service and puts up with a teacher who leads people into the same compromise.

The pressure in these cities was rarely a sword. More often it was a dinner. Trade guilds met at banquets in honour of their gods, and civic festivals honoured the emperor, so refusing could cost a living and a place in the city. Two of these churches face slander and prison, and two are tempted to blend in, and Christ speaks to both with the same seriousness. To Smyrna he says, “Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). Most churches in the comfortable West have more in common with Pergamum than with Smyrna, and it is worth asking which pressure you feel more.

open.label: Revelation 2, passage by passage
open.why: The letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum and Thyatira, passage by passage, with what life in each city was like for the church there.

also.label: The Age of the Martyrs
also.why: What the first Christians in the Roman world faced for refusing to honour the gods and the emperor, told as history.

also.label: Persecution and opposition
also.why: What the whole Bible says to believers who are opposed or mistreated because they follow Jesus.

sessions.question: Which of these four churches sounds most like yours, and which sounds most like you?
sessions.do: Write the pattern of the letters across a page: what Christ sees, what he praises, what he names as wrong, and what he promises. Then write one honest line under each heading for your own church.

verse.text: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will suffer tribulation for ten days. Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.

group.open: Have you ever paid a price, small or large, for refusing to go along with what everyone around you was doing?
discuss: Ephesus got its doctrine right and lost its first love. How does a church, or a person, let that happen without noticing?
Smyrna is poor and Christ calls it rich. What kind of riches does he mean, and how would you recognise them?
The pressure in Pergamum and Thyatira came through work and meals. Where does the same kind of pressure reach you?
group.pray: Pray for your own church by name, giving thanks for what is good in it and asking Christ to correct what he sees that it cannot.

care: Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 3 and the last three churches
teaching: Sardis has a name for being alive, and it is dead. Philadelphia has only a little strength and has kept Christ's word, and to it he gives an open door that no one can shut. Laodicea is the church that thinks it is fine. The city was known for its wealth, and the church has absorbed the city's confidence: “You say, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). Of all seven, it is the only church for which Christ has no word of praise.

The lukewarm water is often read as a scale from on fire to cold, as if cold were better than tepid. One widely held reading, drawn from the cities near Laodicea, hears something else: hot water heals and cold water refreshes, and water that arrives lukewarm does neither. On that reading the charge isn't low enthusiasm. It is uselessness. Then comes the most tender line in the letters, spoken to the worst church of the seven: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3:20). It is often preached to unbelievers, and it can be. But in its place Christ is knocking on the door of a church.

open.label: Revelation 3, passage by passage
open.why: The letters to Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, explained in plain words, with the background of each city.

also.label: Revelation 3, the guided study
also.why: Walk through Revelation 3 in seven steps, noticing what Christ says to each church before deciding what it means.

also.label: Lukewarm faith
also.why: What the Bible says to a faith that has cooled, gathered for anyone who recognises Laodicea in themselves.

sessions.question: Laodicea couldn't see its own poverty. What might you be unable to see about yourself because things are going well?
sessions.do: Read Revelation 3:14 to 22 aloud as if it were addressed to your own church this Sunday. Write down one thing your comfort may be hiding from you, and pray over it for a week.

verse.text: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.

group.open: What is something you only realised you needed after it was taken away?
discuss: Sardis had a name for being alive. What is the difference between a church's reputation and its life?
Philadelphia had little strength and an open door. Why do you think Christ gave that promise to the weak church?
Christ knocks on the door of the church that has shut him out. What does that tell you about him?
group.pray: Ask Christ to show each person, and the whole group, what their comfort hides, and give thanks that he still knocks.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 4 and 5, the throne and the Lamb
teaching: After the letters a door opens in heaven, and before anything else happens on earth John is shown the centre of all things: a throne, and around it living creatures and elders who never stop worshipping. The order matters. The churches have just heard about prison, slander and compromise. Before they see any more of their troubles, they are shown who is actually in charge, and every scene that follows in the book is lit from this room. The empire had its own throne rooms and its own ceremonies of praise for the emperor, and the churches would have heard the difference.

Then comes a scroll that no one can open, and John weeps. An elder tells him that the Lion of the tribe of Judah has triumphed. John turns to see a lion and sees a Lamb, standing, looking as though it had been slain. That is the hinge of the whole book. God's victory over evil looks like a slaughtered lamb, and the new song says why: “You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). The Lamb isn't a stage on the way to the Lion. The Lamb is how the Lion wins.

open.label: Revelation 5, passage by passage
open.why: The scroll, the Lion who is a Lamb, and the new song of heaven, explained in plain words with the Old Testament behind each picture.

also.label: Sacrifice and the Lamb
also.why: Sacrifice through the whole Bible in seven pictures, from the Passover lamb to the Lamb at the centre of the throne in Revelation 5.

also.label: Worship
also.why: What Scripture teaches about worship, from the tabernacle to the throne room John is shown in chapters 4 and 5.

sessions.question: John expected a lion and saw a slain lamb. Where do you still expect God to win the way a lion would?
sessions.do: Read Revelation 4 and 5 aloud and stop at each song. Choose one line from the songs and say it each morning this week before you look at your phone.

verse.text: In a loud voice they were saying: “Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!”

group.open: What song, hymn or piece of music has ever made you feel that something larger than you was true?
discuss: Why do you think the book shows heaven's throne before it shows any more of the trouble on earth?
The elder says lion and John sees a lamb. What does that do to the way we picture power?
The song is sung for people from every tribe, tongue, people and nation. Who would that include that our churches often leave out?
group.pray: Give thanks to the Lamb who was slain, using words from the songs of Revelation 4 and 5 if they help, and ask to see his way of winning more clearly.

sessions.title: Revelation 6 and 7, the seals
teaching: The Lamb opens the seals, and what comes out is the world as people have always known it: conquest, war, famine and death. The four riders aren't horrors kept for a last generation. Jesus spoke of wars, famines and earthquakes as the beginning of birth pains, and the riders show that history, at its worst, is still held on a rein from the throne. At the fifth seal the martyrs cry out, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?” (Revelation 6:10). They are given white robes and told to rest a little longer. Heaven doesn't scold that prayer. It answers it with patience.

Chapter 7 is a pause before the seventh seal. John hears the number of those sealed, a hundred and forty-four thousand from the tribes of Israel, and then he looks and sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (Revelation 7:9). It is the pattern of chapter 5, where he heard of a lion and saw a lamb. Many readers take the counted army and the uncountable crowd to be one people seen two ways, and others read them as two groups. Either way, the chapter ends with the Lamb as shepherd, leading his people to springs of living water.

open.label: Revelation 6, passage by passage
open.why: The four riders, the cry of the martyrs and the great day of wrath, explained in plain words with the Old Testament behind each seal.

also.label: Revelation 7, passage by passage
also.why: The sealing of God's servants and the great multitude in white robes, with the readings of the hundred and forty-four thousand set side by side.

also.label: Hard passages
also.why: Hard passages across the Bible with their notes, including the places in Revelation that trouble careful readers most.

also.label: A blessing for all nations
also.why: From Babel's scattering to the multitude before the throne: the promise to Abraham that Revelation 7 shows fulfilled.

sessions.question: The martyrs pray how long. What would it mean to bring your own how long to God rather than hide it?
sessions.do: Write your own how-long prayer this week, naming something that is wrong and has not been put right. Then read Revelation 7:9 to 17 aloud as the answer heaven gives.

verse.text: For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. ‘He will lead them to springs of living water,’ and ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’

group.open: Where in the news this week did you see something that looked like one of the four riders?
discuss: The riders are released from the throne room. Does it comfort or trouble you that even war and famine are held on God's rein?
Heaven doesn't scold the martyrs for asking how long. What does that say about the prayers God accepts?
John hears a number and sees a crowd beyond counting. What might it mean that God's people are larger than any count we make?
group.pray: Bring before God the places in the world where people are asking how long, and ask that the Lamb would shepherd them to springs of living water.

care: Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 8 to 11, the trumpets and the two witnesses
teaching: The seventh seal opens onto silence in heaven for about half an hour, and then seven trumpets sound. The trumpet plagues echo the plagues of Egypt: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness, locusts. Like Pharaoh's plagues they are warnings meant to turn people back, and they strike a third of things rather than all, which leaves room to repent. The saddest line in the section comes after them: the rest of mankind “still did not repent of the works of their hands” (Revelation 9:20). Judgment in this book is never God losing his temper. It is God refusing to let evil have the last word, and calling people home.

Between the sixth and seventh trumpets comes another pause. John eats a little scroll, sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach, and then two witnesses prophesy, are killed in the street of the great city, and are raised by God. Readers have taken them to be Moses and Elijah, two prophets still to come, or a picture of the whole witnessing church, since the witnesses are called lampstands and chapter 1 has already said the lampstands are the churches. Whichever reading is right, the church's calling is plain: to bear witness when it costs everything. Then the seventh trumpet sounds, and heaven announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ.

open.label: Revelation 11, passage by passage
open.why: The two witnesses and the seventh trumpet, explained in plain words with the main readings of who the witnesses are.

also.label: Judgment
also.why: What Scripture teaches about God's judgment: why it is good news for the wronged, and how it calls people to turn.

also.label: The Exodus
also.why: The Exodus in the Bible's own story, where the plagues on Egypt first appear and the trumpets of Revelation take their shape.

sessions.question: Judgment in this section comes as a warning that leaves room to turn back. What does that tell you about what God wants?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 7 to 10 quickly and Revelation 8 and 9 slowly. Make two columns and match each trumpet to a plague, then note what the echo tells you about God.

verse.text: Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.”

group.open: What is the longest silence you have ever kept, or been kept waiting in?
discuss: The trumpets strike a third of things rather than all of them. Why might the book hold judgment back like that?
People still did not repent after the plagues. Why does suffering alone so rarely change a heart?
If the two witnesses picture the whole church, what would it look like for your church to bear witness the way they do?
group.pray: Pray by name for people you know who are far from God, asking that he would draw them home, and give thanks that the kingdom of the world belongs to Christ.

sessions.title: Revelation 12 and 13, the dragon and the beasts
teaching: Start where the first readers stood. A woman clothed with the sun gives birth to a son who will rule the nations, a great red dragon waits to devour him, and the child is caught up to God. Anyone who knew the Scriptures heard Genesis 3, the serpent and the woman's offspring, and the whole life of Jesus told in a single breath. The dragon is named as “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9). Thrown down to the earth, he turns his rage on the woman's other children, the church. The churches suffer because the dragon is furious, and he is furious because he has already lost.

Then the dragon calls a beast out of the sea, made from the four beasts of Daniel 7 rolled into one, and a second beast from the land makes people worship the first. Seven churches in Roman Asia knew a power that came to them across the sea from Rome, accepted worship, and had local priests and councils to honour it in their own cities. A mark without which no one could buy or sell would have sounded like the guild banquets and festivals they already faced, and many readers see in the beast's number the name Nero Caesar spelled in Hebrew letters. Whatever else the beasts become, they are first a portrait of an empire that makes itself a god, and no age has lacked one.

open.label: Revelation 13, passage by passage
open.why: The two beasts, the mark and the number of the beast, explained in plain words with how the first readers in Roman Asia heard them.

also.label: What did gospel and lord mean under Caesar?
also.why: What words like gospel and lord meant under Caesar, so you hear Revelation's claims the way the churches of Asia heard them.

also.label: The early church under Rome
also.why: How the first Christians lived as a small and suspect people inside the Roman empire, and what the church learned there.

also.label: Daniel 7, passage by passage
also.why: Daniel's four beasts from the sea and the one like a son of man, the vision Revelation 13 gathers into one beast.

sessions.question: What power in your own world asks for the kind of loyalty that belongs only to God?
sessions.do: Read Daniel 7 and then Revelation 13. List what the two chapters share. Then write down one place where you are asked to give something like worship to a power that isn't God.

verse.text: They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death.

group.open: Before reading these chapters, what did the word beast make you picture?
discuss: The dragon rages because he has already been thrown down. How does that change the way you see the church's troubles?
The first readers saw Rome in the beast. Why does it matter to start there before asking what it means for us?
Every age has powers that make themselves gods. Which are hardest for Christians in your setting to see, on the right or on the left?
group.pray: Ask God for clear eyes to see the powers that demand worship, and for courage to give worship to the Lamb alone, together with the church across the world.

care: Some readers are afraid that they have taken the mark without knowing it. In Revelation the mark goes with worshipping the beast and its image (14:9). The chapter speaks of allegiance, of whom a person chooses to worship. If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 14 to 16, the harvest and the bowls
teaching: Chapter 14 answers chapter 13. The beast marks his followers on the hand and the forehead, and the Lamb's people stand with him on Mount Zion with his name and his Father's name on their foreheads. An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel for every nation, tribe, tongue and people, calling them to fear God and give him glory. Then come two harvests, of grain and of grapes trodden in a winepress. Readers differ on whether the first is the gathering of God's people and the second judgment, or whether both are judgment. In the middle comes a line for tired believers: “Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus” (Revelation 14:12).

Before the seven bowls are poured out, those who have conquered the beast stand beside a sea of glass and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, the song of the Red Sea now sung for all the nations: “Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations” (Revelation 15:3). The bowls fall on the kingdom of the beast. They are hard to read, and they ought to be. These chapters have sometimes been used to frighten people, children above all, into faith. They were written to comfort churches that were being crushed, and to assure them that God would not let their oppressors go unanswered.

open.label: Revelation 14, passage by passage
open.why: The Lamb on Mount Zion, the eternal gospel and the two harvests, explained in plain words with the main readings of each.

also.label: Revelation 16, passage by passage
also.why: The seven bowls, with a plain word for anyone frightened by the chapter about whom these judgments are aimed at.

also.label: Is hell forever, or does it end?
also.why: An honest answer to one of the hardest questions these chapters raise, with the main Christian views set out fairly.

also.label: Perseverance
also.why: What the Bible teaches about God keeping his people to the end, the hope behind the book's call to endure.

sessions.question: The book calls the saints to endure in the middle of its hardest chapters. What are you being asked to endure now?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 15:1 to 18 and then Revelation 15:1 to 4. Write down what the two songs share, and keep the second where you will see it this week.

verse.text: Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.

group.open: When have you had to keep going at something long after the reason for it stopped feeling obvious?
discuss: The Lamb's people carry his name where the beast's people carry the mark. What would it mean to belong to him that openly?
The bowls come after a song that praises God's ways as just and true. Why might that order matter?
Some people have been frightened by these chapters since childhood. How would you speak about them to someone who was afraid?
group.pray: Pray for believers who are worn down, near and far, asking God to keep them faithful, and give thanks that his ways are just and true.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 17 and 18, the fall of Babylon
teaching: Babylon appears as a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, glittering with gold, riding the beast and drunk with the blood of the saints. She sits on seven hills, and the first readers knew which city sat on seven hills. Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem's temple and carried God's people into exile, and Peter's first letter seems to use the name for Rome already. Here she stands for a whole way of life: a city of luxury, trade and power that seduces the nations and lives off them.

Chapter 18 is a funeral song, sung by kings, merchants and sailors who mourn the city because they grew rich from her. The list of her cargo runs from gold and cinnamon to horses and chariots and ends with “slaves and souls of men” (Revelation 18:13). That last line is the verdict. An economy that trades in human beings has made itself a god. God's people are not told to storm the city. They are told to leave it: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins” (Revelation 18:4). Most of us live comfortably inside some version of Babylon, and coming out of her is rarely a move of house. It is a change of loyalty.

open.label: Revelation 18, passage by passage
open.why: The fall of Babylon, the laments of kings and merchants, and the cargo list, explained in plain words.

also.label: Idolatry
also.why: What Scripture teaches about idols, including the ones made of money, comfort and power that Babylon offers.

also.label: Why did Jesus treat money as a rival god?
also.why: A guide to money and the heart, for anyone asking what coming out of Babylon looks like in an ordinary budget.

also.label: When the church married empire
also.why: What happened when the church grew comfortable with imperial power, and why Babylon's appeal never quite goes away.

sessions.question: Where do you most enjoy the comforts of Babylon, and what would coming out of her look like for you?
sessions.do: Read the cargo list in Revelation 18:11 to 13. Then look at a week of your own spending and ask of each thing whose labour made it and what it asked of your heart.

verse.text: Then I heard another voice from heaven say: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.”

group.open: What city, real or imagined, has most captured your imagination, and why?
discuss: Babylon is mourned by those who grew rich from her. Who mourns the loss of comfortable power today?
The cargo list ends with human beings. Where does our way of life still trade in people?
Coming out of Babylon is a change of loyalty more than a change of address. What would that change look like in your week?
group.pray: Pray for people who are trapped or used by the world's trade, and ask God for hearts set free from Babylon's charm.

care: A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 19 and 20, the rider and the thousand years
teaching: Heaven breaks into praise over Babylon's fall, and then a rider appears on a white horse. His robe is dipped in blood before any battle begins, his name is The Word of God, and the only weapon named is a sword that comes from his mouth. Many readers take the blood to be his own and the sword to be his word, so that the last victory is won the way the Lamb has always won. These chapters have often been read with a calendar in one hand and the news in the other, and every confident date so far has come and gone. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour” (Matthew 24:36). The book gives the church a hope to live by, and it never gives a timetable.

Chapter 20 speaks of Satan bound and of saints reigning with Christ for a thousand years. Premillennialists, historic and dispensational, expect Christ to return before an earthly reign. Postmillennialists expect the gospel to spread and the world to change before he returns. Amillennialists, following a reading Augustine made widely known, take the thousand years to be the present age, in which Christ reigns and the martyrs reign with him. Faithful Christians who confess the creeds have held each view, and each has verses it finds hard to fit. What none of them doubts is in the same chapter: the dead, great and small, stand before the throne, and evil is ended for good.

open.label: Revelation 20, passage by passage
open.why: Satan bound, the thousand years and the last judgment, explained in plain words with the main millennial views set side by side.

also.label: Which view am I?
also.why: Short which-view quizzes, including one on the end times and the millennium, to see where your own instincts lie and why.

also.label: The last things
also.why: The doctrine of the last things: Christ's return, the resurrection, judgment and the views of the millennium, set out fairly.

also.label: Christ's return
also.why: What the Bible teaches about Christ's return, the one hope every millennial view shares.

sessions.question: Christians who share the creed read the thousand years differently. What would it ask of you to hold your own view with both conviction and humility?
sessions.do: Read Revelation 20 slowly and write each of the three views in a sentence of your own. Then write down what all three confess together.

verse.text: And I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude, like the rushing of many waters, and like a mighty rumbling of thunder, crying out: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.”

group.open: What were you first taught about the end times, and how did it leave you feeling?
discuss: The rider's robe is bloodied before the battle and his weapon is his word. What does that say about how Christ wins?
Which millennial view are you drawn to, and what is the strongest point of the view you find hardest?
All the views agree that Christ returns, the dead are raised and evil ends. Why might that be enough to stand on together?
group.pray: Give thanks that the Lord God Almighty reigns, and ask for patience and charity among Christians who read this chapter differently.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Revelation 21 and 22, all things made new
teaching: The book that began with seven struggling churches ends with a city coming down out of heaven, and the direction matters. People don't climb away from the earth to reach God. God comes to dwell with people, and the one seated on the throne says, “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5). He doesn't make all new things. He makes all things new. Tears are wiped away, and death and mourning are no more. There is no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, and the city itself is a perfect cube, the shape of the most holy place.

The last chapter returns to the first pages of the Bible. A river flows from the throne, and on either side stands the tree of life, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in Eden is given back larger than before: a garden has become a city, and two people have become a multitude from every nation. The book doesn't end with a date. It ends with a prayer, “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20), one of the oldest prayers of the church and the only fitting one for anyone who has read this far. What the church confesses about that hope, and why, is where the Academy goes next.

open.label: Revelation 21, passage by passage
open.why: The new heaven and new earth, the holy city and the end of tears, explained in plain words with the Old Testament promises behind them.

also.label: The life to come
also.why: The Christian hope in seven pictures: death named honestly, the body raised, a just judgment, and all things made new.

also.label: The new creation
also.why: The last act of the Bible's story, where everything from Genesis onward is gathered into the new heaven and the new earth.

also.label: The Apostles' Creed
also.why: Go on in the Academy to the Apostles' Creed: what the church confesses about Christ's return, the resurrection and the life everlasting.

sessions.question: Revelation ends with God coming to live with his people rather than people escaping to him. How does that change what you hope for?
sessions.do: Read Revelation 21 and 22 aloud slowly. Write down one thing on earth you love and one thing that breaks your heart, and beside each, what these chapters promise about it.

verse.text: And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”

group.open: What is the most beautiful place you have ever seen, and what made it so?
discuss: The city comes down from heaven to earth. How is that different from the picture of heaven you grew up with?
The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. What do you long to see healed?
The book ends with the prayer Come, Lord Jesus. What would it mean for you to pray it and mean it?
group.pray: Give thanks for the promise that God will dwell with his people and wipe away every tear, and then pray, each in your own words, for Christ to come.

care: If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
